subject: 덕은 가르칠 수 있는가
title: Whether virtue can be taught
content: An old question in moral philosophy asks whether virtue is the sort of thing that can be taught, and the question is sharper than it looks. Skills are taught by instruction and practice, and there are recognized teachers of them, whereas nobody advertises as a teacher of justice and the children of just people are not reliably just. If virtue were knowledge, this pattern would be puzzling. One response holds that virtue is indeed knowledge but of an unusual kind, since knowing what courage requires in a particular situation is not a rule that can be handed over. It is a capacity for judgment, and such capacities are developed by acting under guidance rather than by being told. On this view virtue is taught, though not in the manner of arithmetic. A second response denies that instruction is central at all. Character forms through habituation, so a person becomes generous by performing generous acts until the disposition settles, and the role of a teacher is to arrange the practice rather than to convey a doctrine. This explains why moral argument rarely changes conduct while sustained example often does. Both responses agree that telling someone what is right accomplishes less than we expect, and much moral education proceeds on that assumption whether or not it is stated.

subject: 관찰은 이론에 물드는가
title: Whether observation is shaped by theory
content: Observation was long treated as the neutral ground on which theories are tested, and philosophy of science has questioned that picture. Two scientists holding different theories may look at the same instrument and report different things, not because either is careless but because what counts as relevant, and even what registers as a single event, depends on what the observer expects. A trained radiologist sees a lesion where a novice sees a smudge. If observation is shaped in this way, then the neutrality that made it decisive is compromised, since a theory could protect itself by shaping the very reports that might refute it. Some conclude that theory choice is therefore not rationally determined by evidence, and that scientific change involves persuasion as much as proof. Defenders of evidence answer that the dependence is real and limited. Observers with opposed theories do agree about a great deal, instruments produce records that outlast any interpretation, and the history of science contains many cases where data forced a change nobody wanted. What follows is that observation is corrigible rather than neutral, which is weaker than the old picture and strong enough to do the work that testing requires.

subject: 고대 도시의 배수와 도로 포장
title: Drains and paving in the ancient city
content: Excavated ancient streets often show several surfaces stacked one above another, each laid over the accumulated refuse of the previous one. The sequence records a city that rose steadily above its own debris, and it dates the interventions, since a new pavement can be tied to the layers it seals. Where a street was repaved often, the community had both the means and the reason to maintain it. Drainage appears alongside paving rather than separately. Channels run beneath the surface or along its edge, and their gradients were surveyed carefully enough to carry water out of the settlement, which required knowing the fall across the whole built area. Such works could not be undertaken by a single household, so their presence indicates an authority able to coordinate and to fund. What the archaeology also shows is where this failed. Quarters away from the main routes keep beaten earth for centuries, and the refuse layers there are thicker, which indicates that paving and drainage followed the interests of whoever paid rather than the needs of the whole ancient population. Historians reading an excavated street plan therefore treat surface quality as a map of investment, and the untouched quarters as evidence about who was not being served.

subject: 진리는 대응인가 정합인가
title: Truth as correspondence or as coherence
content: A statement is true, on one account, when it corresponds to how things are, and this seems less a theory than a statement of the obvious. Philosophy has nevertheless found the account hard to develop, because saying what correspondence consists in requires identifying the things that statements correspond to, and no candidate has proved satisfactory. Facts introduced for the purpose look suspiciously like shadows of the statements themselves. A rival account locates truth in coherence, holding that a belief is true when it fits with the rest of a well-organized system. This avoids the difficulty about correspondence and generates its own, since a consistent fiction would then count as true, and coherence alone cannot distinguish a well-built story from an accurate one. Defenders add constraints about observation, which brings the world back in through another door. A third position treats the whole dispute as inflated. On this view calling a statement true adds nothing to asserting it, so no substantial theory is required and the appearance of a deep question comes from treating a grammatical form as naming a property. Critics reply that truth does explanatory work in accounts of meaning and inquiry, which a merely grammatical view cannot supply.

subject: 선사 토기의 태토와 산지 추적
title: Prehistoric pottery and where its clay came from
content: The clay body of a prehistoric pot carries mineral inclusions that reflect the geology of the place it was dug, and thin sections cut from a sherd let archaeologists identify those inclusions under a microscope. Where the minerals of a vessel do not match the geology around the site that yielded it, the pot travelled or its maker did. This method has redrawn the map of prehistoric contact. Vessels once assumed to be local turn out to come from many kilometres away, and the distances involved are often greater than the settlement pattern would suggest. Equally informative are cases where the form is foreign and the clay is local, since that combination indicates a potter copying a shape she had seen rather than a pot arriving. The technique has limits worth stating. Some regions share geology across wide areas, so a match cannot establish a specific source, and clay was sometimes carried a short distance before being worked. Archaeologists therefore combine the mineral evidence with chemical analysis of trace elements, and they report a source region rather than a village. What the two methods together establish is that prehistoric communities were connected far more widely than the older reconstructions allowed.

subject: 의미는 머릿속에 있는가
title: Whether meaning is in the head
content: It seems natural to suppose that what a word means is fixed by what its speaker has in mind, so that two people in identical mental states must mean the same thing by the same word. Philosophy of language has argued against this, and the argument has consequences that reach well beyond semantics. Imagine two speakers alike in every psychological respect, one on Earth and one in an environment where the clear liquid in rivers has a different chemical composition. Each uses the word water, each associates the same appearances with it, and yet each refers to a different substance, because what a term picks out depends partly on the environment in which it was learned. Meaning therefore is not determined by what is inside the speaker. The conclusion has been extended to mental states themselves. If a belief is about water rather than the other substance, then the content of that belief depends on the speaker's surroundings, so thoughts are individuated partly by the world. Critics find this counterintuitive and observe that it complicates any account of how beliefs cause behaviour, since two identically behaving speakers would hold different beliefs. Defenders answer that the alternative severs language from the world it is used to talk about.

subject: 생물학적 종 개념의 다원성
title: Why biology has several species concepts
content: Biologists use more than one definition of species, and these definitions do not always agree about where the lines fall. One defines a species by breeding isolation, another by shared descent, and a third by the role it plays in a habitat, and each was framed because the others failed somewhere. Asexual organisms have no breeding isolation to appeal to, fossils cannot be tested for interbreeding, and groups that never meet cannot be judged either way. Philosophy of biology has asked whether this plurality is a passing state of ignorance or a lasting feature. Those who expect one answer hold that a mature science will settle on a single test, so the present variety shows only that we do not yet know enough. Those who defend the plurality argue that species are not one kind of thing, so different concepts track patterns that are genuinely different, and forcing them together would hide what each one catches. This dispute matters outside the seminar. Conservation law protects species, so the definition chosen decides which groups get protection and which do not, and the choice can settle the fate of a population that one test counts as distinct while another does not. Biologists making such calls therefore work with a concept whose ground is still argued over.

subject: 고대의 염전과 소금 생산 유적
title: Ancient salt works and what they left behind
content: Salt does not survive in the archaeological record, and yet the places where it was made are among the most visible ancient industrial sites. Production by boiling brine required vast quantities of coarse ceramic containers, which were used once and broken, so the debris mounds beside such works can cover hectares and rise several metres. Archaeologists identify these sites by the fabric of the sherds rather than by any surviving product. What the mounds record is scale. The number of vessels implies output far beyond local consumption, so the salt travelled, and the distribution of the distinctive ceramic fabric traces how far. Where solar evaporation was used instead, the traces are subtler, consisting of shallow basins and channels that survey and aerial photography reveal in coastal landscapes. Both methods left landscapes that were shaped for one purpose. The ancient importance of salt lay in preservation. Meat and fish kept through a winter only if salted, so a community without access to it was limited in what it could store, and the routes carrying salt inland appear in the archaeology before many other kinds of exchange. Historians therefore treat these production sites as evidence about food storage and settlement rather than about any luxury.

subject: 설명적 깊이란 무엇인가
title: What makes one explanation deeper than another
content: Some explanations satisfy us and others leave the question standing, even when both are true and both cite causes. Philosophy of science has tried to say what the difference consists in, since scientific progress is often described as achieving deeper explanations rather than merely more of them. One proposal appeals to unification. An explanation is deeper when it derives many phenomena from few assumptions, so a theory covering falling apples and orbiting moons explains more deeply than separate accounts of each. This captures a real virtue and it does not obviously distinguish depth from breadth. A second proposal appeals to counterfactual reach. An explanation is deeper when it tells us what would have happened under a wider range of alternative conditions, so a mechanism that answers many what-if questions explains more deeply than one that answers few. This fits scientific practice, where understanding is demonstrated by predicting behaviour under intervention. Both proposals treat depth as relative to a range of questions rather than as a property of the explanation alone. That relativity strikes some as a defect and others as an accurate description, since what counts as a satisfying answer plainly depends on what was being asked.

subject: 고대 도시의 시장 광장과 집회
title: The open square in the ancient city
content: Many ancient cities contain a large open space near their centre, and excavation shows these squares serving several purposes at once. Traders set up temporary stalls whose post holes survive, assemblies gathered where the ground was levelled and sometimes stepped, and the buildings around the edge housed offices whose functions the inscriptions record. The square was not specialized, and that is the point. Its physical development can be dated. Early phases show an unpaved area with buildings encroaching on it, later phases show the boundary fixed and the surface laid, and the intervention that fixed it usually coincides with other evidence of an authority asserting itself. Once defined, such spaces proved remarkably stable, and the outline of an ancient square often survives in the street plan of the modern town above it. What the square made possible was assembly at a scale that no building could hold. A community that could gather in one place could also be addressed in one place, so the space served rulers and crowds alike, and the ancient sources record it as the setting for both proclamation and revolt. Archaeologists reading its development therefore treat it as political architecture rather than as leftover ground.

subject: 개념 공학 — 개념을 바꿔야 할 때
title: Repairing the concepts we reason with
content: Philosophy has traditionally analysed concepts, asking what knowledge or justice actually is. A newer approach asks a different question, namely whether the concept we have is the one we should be using, and it treats concepts as tools that can be improved rather than as objects to be described. This shift is called conceptual engineering. The motivation is straightforward. Some concepts do their work badly, drawing distinctions that mislead or grouping cases that ought to be separated, and a careful analysis of such a concept merely describes a defective instrument. Where a concept plays a role in law or in moral judgment, its defects have consequences, so revising it may be more useful than mapping it. Objections concentrate on two points. The first is that changing a concept risks changing the subject, so that a revised notion of knowledge is no longer an account of knowledge but of something else, and the questions we cared about remain unanswered. The second is practical, since concepts are held by communities and no philosopher can simply legislate a change. Defenders answer that concepts do shift under pressure from argument, and that engineering describes something that has always happened rather than proposing something new.

subject: 허구적 대상에 대한 진술
title: Statements about things that do not exist
content: We say confidently that a fictional detective lived in London and that he did not exist, and both statements seem true although they appear to conflict. Philosophy of language has asked how a name that refers to nothing can appear in true sentences, and the answers proposed differ in what they are willing to accept. One approach admits fictional objects into the inventory of what there is, treating them as abstract entities created by authors much as symphonies are. Statements about them are then straightforwardly true or false. The cost is a population of objects that many find extravagant, and a puzzle about how an abstract entity could be described as living anywhere. A second approach denies any such objects and analyses the statements as being about the story rather than about a person. To say that the detective lived in London is to say that the story represents it so, and the apparent conflict dissolves because the two claims operate at different levels. Critics observe that the paraphrase is awkward for statements comparing characters across works, and that readers do not seem to be talking about texts when they discuss a character. The dispute continues because each account handles cleanly what the other handles badly.

subject: 고대 문명의 벽돌 규격과 건축
title: Standard bricks in ancient building
content: Bricks recovered from ancient sites are often uniform in size across a whole settlement and across long periods, and the dimensions differ between regions in ways that let archaeologists date and attribute construction from the bricks alone. Where a building uses a size unknown in its area, either the material was moved or the builders came from elsewhere. Standardization made construction faster and more predictable. A mason working with known dimensions can calculate quantities before beginning, and courses laid to a fixed module produce walls whose stability does not depend on individual judgment. The proportions chosen also matter, since a brick twice as long as it is wide allows bonding patterns that a square one does not, and ancient builders arrived at such ratios in several regions independently. What changes in the sequence tell us about is organization rather than technique. A shift to a new standard across many buildings at once indicates a decision taken centrally, and the appearance of stamped bricks bearing an official mark shows production being supervised. Archaeologists therefore read brick dimensions as administrative evidence, and a site where sizes vary building by building as one where construction was arranged household by household.

subject: 집단은 믿음을 가질 수 있는가
title: Whether a group can believe anything
content: We say that a committee believes a proposal is sound or that a company knew of a risk, and philosophy asks whether such statements describe anything beyond the beliefs of individuals. The question has practical weight, since holding an organization responsible for what it knew presupposes that it could know something. A reductive answer treats group belief as shorthand for the beliefs of members, perhaps of most of them or of those in authority. This keeps the metaphysics simple and it fails on a familiar case, because a committee can be committed to a conclusion that no member accepts, arising from voting on the premises separately. The group's position is then genuinely its own. A non-reductive answer accepts group belief as a distinct state, grounded in a joint commitment to reason and act as if the proposition were true. On this view the committee's belief is real and its members may privately dissent without contradiction. Critics object that this stretches belief beyond recognition, since believing is supposed to involve conviction rather than commitment. Defenders reply that the state does the work belief does, guiding inference and grounding responsibility, and that the label matters less than the role.

subject: 선사 암각화의 분포와 이동로
title: Rock art and the routes it marks
content: Prehistoric carvings and paintings are not scattered at random across a landscape, and this fact has shaped how archaeologists read them. They cluster at passes, at river crossings, at the mouths of valleys, and at points with a wide view, so the distribution is read alongside the routes that people would have taken. A panel at a pass therefore marks a place where travellers had to go. Establishing that such placement is deliberate requires ruling out the obvious alternative, namely that art survives where the rock is suitable and the weather is kind. Systematic survey has addressed this by recording surfaces without art as well as those with it, and the results show carved panels concentrated at movement points beyond what rock type alone would predict. This pattern holds across several regions studied in the same way. What the art meant at such places nevertheless remains open. Proposals include marking territory, recording a journey, and addressing whatever was thought to inhabit a threshold, and the evidence rarely separates them. What the distribution does establish is that these communities moved along predictable paths and treated certain points as requiring a mark, which is a conclusion about prehistoric landscape use rather than about belief.

subject: 희망은 합리적일 수 있는가
title: Whether hope can be rational
content: Hoping for an outcome involves wanting it and believing it possible, and these two components seem to exhaust the state until one notices that hope can be criticized in ways neither explains. A person may hope against evidence, and we sometimes call this foolish and sometimes admirable, which suggests that assessing hope involves more than checking the probability. Philosophy has asked what standards apply. One account holds that hope is rational when the desire is appropriate and the belief in possibility is accurate, however small the chance. On this view a patient who hopes for recovery against long odds does nothing irrational, since she believes only that recovery is possible, and she is right. Critics answer that this misses how hope directs attention and effort, since a hope that consumes a life is not vindicated by being logically permissible. A second account attends to the role hope plays. Hoping sustains action where certainty is unavailable, so a hope that enables someone to continue is doing something valuable that a bare probability estimate cannot. What follows is that hope may be assessed practically as well as epistemically, and the two assessments can come apart, which is why we sometimes admire a hope we would not share.

subject: 죽음이 나쁜 이유
title: Why death is bad for the one who dies
content: Most people regard death as a misfortune for the person who dies, and an ancient argument denies that it can be. Harm requires a subject who suffers it, and once a person is dead there is no subject, so there is no time at which death is bad for her. She is not harmed while alive, since she is not yet dead, and not harmed afterward, since she does not exist. The argument is short and its conclusion is hard to accept. The most common reply appeals to deprivation. Death is bad because it takes away the goods a person would otherwise have had, and this harm does not require a moment at which it is felt, any more than a betrayal one never learns of requires being noticed to be a wrong. Comparing what happened with what would have happened is enough. Critics press two difficulties. The comparison requires knowing what the alternative would have been, which is often indeterminate, and the account implies that we should regard the time before our birth as an equivalent deprivation, which almost nobody does. Defenders answer this second point by arguing that a person could have lived longer but could not have been born earlier and remained the same person.

subject: 중세 도시의 상수 공급과 우물
title: Wells and water supply in the medieval town
content: Medieval towns drew water from wells, from streams, and in some places from conduits that brought it in from springs beyond the walls. Excavation locates the wells precisely, since the shafts were lined and often survive intact, and their distribution shows how far a household had to walk. Where wells are close together the population was dense, and where a quarter has none the residents were carrying water from elsewhere. Contamination was the central problem and the archaeology records it. Wells sunk near cesspits show it in the deposits at their base, and the surviving town ordinances forbid exactly the practices the excavated evidence reveals, which indicates that the rules addressed a real and persistent situation. Communities understood that some water made people ill without knowing why, and they responded by regulating placement rather than treatment. Conduits changed the picture where they were built. A piped supply from an outside spring delivered water that had not passed through the town, and the medieval accounts of such works show them funded by religious houses or wealthy citizens and maintained with difficulty. Archaeologists trace the pipe runs and find them repaired repeatedly, which tells us both that the water mattered and that keeping it flowing was a continuing struggle.

subject: 세대 간 인구 윤리의 역설
title: A paradox in thinking about future populations
content: Comparing outcomes that differ in how many people exist turns out to generate conclusions that almost nobody accepts. If a larger population with lives barely worth living can be better than a smaller one with excellent lives, merely because the total of well-being is greater, then the arithmetic recommends something repugnant. Yet the assumptions that produce this result are individually plausible. Each says only that adding a life worth living does not make an outcome worse, that a small loss for many can outweigh a large gain for few, and that these comparisons are transitive. Rejecting any one of them carries a cost elsewhere, and philosophers have spent decades establishing that the costs are real. Several impossibility results now show that no ranking of populations satisfies all the conditions we would want. What follows is disputed. Some conclude that our intuitions about large numbers are unreliable and should yield to the arithmetic, while others conclude that aggregation itself is the mistake and that well-being does not sum across persons. A third response accepts that the theory is incomplete and continues to use it where the comparisons are less extreme, which is how most practical work proceeds.

subject: 초기 농경민의 저장 구덩이
title: Storage pits of the earliest farmers
content: Pits dug into the subsoil are among the commonest features on early farming sites, and establishing what they held has taken careful work. Grain stored in a sealed pit consumes the oxygen near its surface and creates conditions in which the rest keeps for a year or more, and experimental reconstruction has confirmed that the method works when the pit is properly sealed. Charred grain recovered from the fill often comes from the burning that sterilized the pit before reuse. What the pits reveal is a change in how a community handled time. A household that could store a harvest could survive a poor season and could plant more than it needed immediately, whereas one that consumed as it reaped could not. The number and capacity of pits at a site therefore indicate how far ahead these early farmers were able to plan. Their placement matters as well. Pits inside individual house compounds indicate storage held by households, whereas clusters in a common area indicate something managed collectively, and sites show both arrangements. Archaeologists read this difference as evidence about who controlled the surplus, and the shift from one pattern to the other at some sites marks a change in social organization rather than in agriculture.

subject: 악은 설명될 수 있는가
title: Whether evil admits of explanation
content: Explaining a terrible act seems to risk excusing it, and this worry has made some people resist explanation altogether. Moral philosophy distinguishes the two, since accounting for how something came about is a different operation from justifying it, and no amount of causal detail entails that an act was permissible. The resistance nevertheless points at something real. What it points at is the fear that understanding dissolves responsibility. If a person's cruelty is fully explained by upbringing and circumstance, then blaming her may seem to blame a process rather than an agent, and our practices of censure rest on treating her as the author of what she did. This is the problem of moral luck appearing in another form. Two responses are available. The first holds that explanation and responsibility operate at different levels, so a complete causal story leaves the moral assessment untouched, much as explaining a proof does not make it invalid. The second accepts some erosion of blame while insisting that condemnation of the act survives. Both preserve the practical conclusion that understanding is necessary, since preventing such acts requires knowing how they arise, and refusing to look is a poor tribute to those they harmed.

subject: 심신 인과의 문제
title: How mental states could cause anything
content: A decision seems to cause an action. Yet every physical event appears to have a sufficient physical cause, so the mental state risks being left with nothing to do. Philosophy of mind calls this the problem of mental causation, and it arises for any view that treats the mental as distinct while insisting that thoughts make a difference. The obvious escape identifies mental states with physical ones. A decision then just is a brain state, and its causal work becomes unproblematic. This preserves causation, although it struggles with the observation that the same mental state could be realized in very different physical systems, which suggests that the mental kind is not identical to any single physical kind. A second escape holds that mental properties depend on physical ones without being identical to them. They then inherit causal relevance from what they depend on. Critics reply that this leaves the mental doing no work of its own, since the physical base was already sufficient. The most developed responses argue that causal relevance is a matter of which differences would have mattered, and that mental descriptions capture patterns which the physical ones would obscure.

subject: 중세 촌락의 방앗간과 공동 설비
title: Mills and shared equipment in the medieval village
content: A watermill needed a weir, a channel to carry water, a wheel, and gearing, and the whole cost far more than a peasant household could raise. Medieval mills were therefore built by lords, by monasteries, or by villages acting together, and the dug remains show how much earth even a modest one demanded. The water channel is often the clearest surviving feature. Because the mill was costly, its owner commonly required that villagers grind there rather than at home, so the surviving records are full of quarrels about hand querns, which manor courts seized and broke. Archaeologists find those fragments in exactly the deposits the documents would predict. The duty turned a technical edge into a claim on the harvest, and the anger it raised appears again and again in the medieval record. Where villages held the mill themselves, the arrangements look different. Accounts show upkeep shared and turns rotated, and the quarrels concern timing rather than compulsion. Historians therefore read the medieval mill as a case where one technology produced opposite social outcomes depending on who paid for it, and the archaeology of the building alone cannot tell the two apart.

subject: 은유는 인지적 내용을 갖는가
title: Whether metaphor says anything
content: A metaphor asserts something literally false, and yet we treat many metaphors as illuminating rather than as mistakes. Philosophy of language has asked whether a metaphor carries content that could in principle be stated plainly, or whether its effect is of a different kind altogether. The answer bears on how much of our reasoning is figurative. One view holds that a metaphor means something, namely whatever the corresponding simile would assert, so understanding it is grasping a comparison. This makes metaphor analysable and it flattens what many find valuable, since a good metaphor seems to do something a comparison does not, and paraphrases are notoriously disappointing. A second view denies that metaphors have any meaning beyond the literal one. On this account the sentence says what its words say, which is false, and its power lies in what it makes the hearer notice rather than in what it states. This explains why paraphrase fails, since there was never a second meaning to capture. Critics object that it leaves metaphor outside the space of reasons, unable to support inference, while much scientific and moral thinking appears to proceed through figures that do support it.
